title: Maynard–Tao multidimensional sieve over the (c,d) certificate grid
connection: Maynard–Tao weights (Σλ_{d1..dk})² detect many simultaneous 'prime/structured' events among k linear forms; the ES Type I certificate grid offers many linear-in-(c,d) objects at fixed p (e.g. moduli 4cd, values p²+4c²d).
why: MT weights produce 'at least m of k events happen' from first-moment data only — the shape we want for 'at least one certificate fires' — and here the average is over (c,d) at a single fixed p.
first_step: Write the k-tuple of events E_j = '4c_jd_j·(stuff) has a divisor ≡ −p mod 4c_jd_j' for an admissible family of (c_j,d_j) = (c0+jh, d0) and compute the MT ratio Σ_j S_j / S_0 numerically at p ~ 10^6.
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)
BRAINSTORM/technique_transfer_list.md §1

title: Maynard 'dense clusters of primes in subsets' for certificate families
connection: Maynard (Compositio 2016) shows any positive-density subset of admissible linear forms contains many simultaneously prime values; ES certificates are indexed by a dense set of linear forms in the C-parameter (4Cp+1, Cp+...).
why: Gives a combinatorial robustness: we need not control which certificate fires, only that a dense sub-family of forms is admissible at p.
first_step: Check whether the family {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} with the divisor-in-class event can be recast as primality of auxiliary linear forms f = (4Cp+1)/d for d in a fixed finite set; test admissibility mod small primes.
refs: Maynard, Dense clusters of primes in subsets, Compositio Math. 152 (2016)

title: Zhang / Polymath8 smooth-moduli level of distribution with modulus 4C smooth
connection: Zhang and Polymath8a get primes equidistributed in APs to smooth moduli beyond x^{1/2}; in ES Type I the tied modulus 4C (or 4cd) is free to be chosen smooth.
why: Choosing C among smooth numbers gives well-factorable moduli, which is exactly where beyond-1/2 equidistribution (dispersion + Kloosterman) is available.
first_step: Restrict the ES Type I/II search to C that are y-smooth (y = log^2 p) and measure on data whether R(p) restricted to smooth C keeps the log^2 p main term (p ≤ 10^7).
refs: Zhang, Bounded gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 179 (2014)
Polymath, Variants of the Selberg sieve…, Res. Math. Sci. 1 (2014)

title: Maynard 'Primes in APs to large moduli I–III' with p-dependent residue class
connection: Maynard (2020) extends Bombieri–Vinogradov-type results to moduli up to x^{3/5} for fixed residue classes and (part III) to uniform residue classes; ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in classes −p mod 4C that move with p.
why: Part III's uniformity in the residue class is exactly the feature a p-dependent class needs.
first_step: Read Maynard 'Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli III: uniform residue classes' and write the ES Type II count Σ_e #{ab | (p+e)/4 : a ≡ −b mod e} as a sum over moduli with residue a(p); identify which theorem shape is needed.
refs: Maynard, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli I, arXiv:2006.06572

title: Lichtman beyond-square-root Goldbach/AP methods for tied moduli
connection: Lichtman (2023) improves level of distribution for primes in APs with well-factorable weights to x^{0.617…} and uses it for Goldbach-type counts; ES Type I/II counts are linear-sieve-like sums over moduli 4C.
why: Any improvement in the level for the ES counting function shrinks the exceptional set exponent (repo's E(N) ≪ N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})).
first_step: Check whether Lichtman's well-factorable weights can be placed on the C-variable (4C | modulus) in the repo's exceptional-set argument (paper/es-threequarter-note.tex).
refs: Lichtman, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli and Goldbach beyond the square-root barrier, arXiv:2309.08522

title: Fouvry–Radziwiłł level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions
connection: Fouvry–Radziwiłł show α*β with one short factor has level of distribution beyond 1/2 for all residue classes; ES divisor counts 1_{ab|N} are convolutions with one short divisor.
why: ES certificates typically use a small divisor a and a large cofactor — the unbalanced regime FR handle.
first_step: Express the Type II e-slice count as Σ_{a small} Σ_{b} 1_{ab = N} with class conditions and check whether FR's theorem (moduli to x^{1/2+δ}) applies when averaging over p in the exceptional-set argument.
refs: Fouvry–Radziwiłł, Level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions, arXiv:1811.08672

title: Guth–Maynard large values of Dirichlet polynomials → short-interval exceptional sets
connection: Guth–Maynard (2024) improve zero-density (Ingham 12/5 → 30/13) via large-values estimates; ES exceptional-set bounds pass through prime counts in short intervals/APs.
why: Zero-density improvements translate to shorter intervals where almost all ES-good primes are detected; could sharpen E(N) or the size of windows where every prime is covered.
first_step: Locate in the repo's exceptional-set notes which zero-density exponent is used and recompute the window exponent with A = 30/13.
refs: Guth–Maynard, New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, arXiv:2405.20552

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł at fixed p along the C-progression
connection: MR show bounded multiplicative functions have the same mean in almost all short intervals as in long ones; the integers 4Cp+1 (C varying) form an AP of modulus 4p at fixed p.
why: A short-AP version (Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen) could show divisor-class statistics of 4Cp+1 in short C-windows match long averages for one fixed p — pointwise in p, average over C.
first_step: Check whether Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen 'multiplicative functions in short arithmetic progressions' covers modulus q = 4p with interval length X = p^{θ}; compute what θ the ES Type I count needs.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), arXiv:1501.04585

title: Tao entropy decrement in the C-variable at fixed p
connection: Tao's entropy decrement (log-Chowla two-point, Erdős discrepancy) shows that at most scales the residues of n mod small primes behave independently of the random variable studied; here the random variable is C ↦ 4Cp+1 with p fixed.
why: It converts correlations into averages with a free prime shift — and at fixed p the average over C is legitimate (no averaging over p).
first_step: Formulate: random C ≤ X, X_C = (divisibility pattern of 4Cp+1 by primes ≤ H); compute the empirical mutual information I(X_C ; C mod ℓ) for p = a hard prime from DISPROOF_AVENUES.md.
refs: Tao, The logarithmically averaged Chowla and Elliott conjectures for two-point correlations, arXiv:1509.05422

title: Helfgott–Radziwiłł expansion of divisibility graphs
connection: Helfgott–Radziwiłł (2021) prove expansion of graphs on integers where n ~ n+p if p | n (prime p in a range), improving log-Chowla; ES witnesses are divisibility relations d | N with N in a p-tied family.
why: A divisibility-graph expander on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} could transport 'some witness' along edges, the kind of local-to-global step ES lacks.
first_step: Build the graph on C ≤ 10^5 (fixed p) with edges C ~ C' if a common prime ℓ ≤ H divides both 4Cp+1 and 4C'p+1 and compute its spectral gap.
refs: Helfgott–Radziwiłł, Expansion, divisibility and parity, arXiv:2103.06853

title: Pilatte two-point log-Chowla improvement via graph spectra
connection: Pilatte (2023) gets (log X)^{−c} savings for two-point log Chowla using spectral bounds for random-like graphs on integers; same graph-on-divisibility template as Helfgott–Radziwiłł.
why: Quantitative spectral inputs are what a fixed-p C-average argument would need.
first_step: Read Pilatte's graph construction and check whether its vertex set can be replaced by an AP {4Cp+1}.
refs: Pilatte, Improved bounds for the two-point logarithmic Chowla conjecture, arXiv:2310.19357

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao higher uniformity in short intervals
connection: MRT (Annals 2023) prove Gowers/nilsequence uniformity of bounded multiplicative functions in almost all short intervals; ES counts are correlations of multiplicative-type indicator functions along affine forms in C.
why: Uniformity norms control linear-form correlations — e.g. Σ_C 1_{d | 4Cp+1}·1_{class}.
first_step: Write the C-average of the Type I indicator as a correlation of multiplicative functions along linear forms in C and identify which Gowers norm controls it.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao–Teräväinen–Ziegler, Higher uniformity of bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals on average, arXiv:2007.15644

title: Matthiesen: linear correlations of divisor-type functions
connection: Matthiesen proves asymptotics for correlations of multiplicative functions such as τ, r_2 along systems of linear forms (via Green–Tao nilsequence machinery); ES solution counts at varying (c,d) are such correlations of class-restricted divisor functions.
why: Gives asymptotics with main terms for averaged ES counts over linear families, potentially over thinner families than ET's.
first_step: Check whether 'number of divisors ≡ −1 mod q' restricted divisor functions satisfy Matthiesen's hypotheses (they are not multiplicative but are sums over characters mod q of multiplicative functions).
refs: Matthiesen, Linear correlations of multiplicative functions, arXiv:1606.04482

title: Green–Sawhney 'primes of the form p²+nq²' bilinear technique for p²+4c²d
connection: Green–Sawhney (2024) count primes of the form p² + nq² with p,q prime using Type I/II bilinear sieve on a binary quadratic form; ES Type I concerns divisors of p² + 4c²d, values of the same form shape.
why: Their Type II information on x² + n y² over thin variables is closely aligned with ES's quadratic value p² + 4c²d at fixed p.
first_step: Read Green–Sawhney's Type II estimate and check whether it gives equidistribution of divisors of p² + 4c²d in residue classes mod 4cd when c,d range over boxes at fixed p.
refs: Green–Sawhney, Primes of the form p^2 + nq^2, arXiv:2410.04189

title: Friedlander–Iwaniec asymptotic sieve (x²+y⁴) for thin certificate families
connection: FI breaks parity for primes x²+y⁴ via bilinear forms on a thin quadratic sequence; ES Type I with d a square gives p² + (2cy)², sums of two squares.
why: Restricting to d = y² makes the Type I object a Gaussian norm, where FI-type bilinear technology is designed to work.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^7, the fraction of primes with an ES Type I certificate having d a perfect square, and whether it stays bounded below.
refs: Friedlander–Iwaniec, The polynomial X^2+Y^4 captures its primes, Ann. Math. 148 (1998)

title: Heath-Brown x³+2y³ cubic parity breaking analogue for norm-form certificates
connection: Heath-Brown's primes of the form x³+2y³ use a Type II estimate on a cubic norm form; ES certificates can be written as divisors of norms from Q(√−d) at fixed p.
why: A norm-form viewpoint replaces 'divisor in residue class' by 'ideal in ray class', where parity-breaking for norm forms exists.
first_step: Write the Type I certificate as: an ideal 𝔞 | (p + 2c√−d) with N𝔞 ≡ −p mod 4cd, i.e. a ray-class condition, and list the ray class field.
refs: Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x^3+2y^3, Acta Math. 186 (2001)

title: Maynard 'primes represented by incomplete norm forms' for ES norm forms
connection: Maynard (Forum Pi 2020) counts primes as norms N(a1ω1+…+akωk) with missing coordinates, using a sieve beyond classical parity; ES Type I divisor event is a norm-divisibility event in quadratic fields.
why: Incomplete-norm-form technology handles thin sets of algebraic integers, relevant to certificates where only a few coordinates vary (c,d at fixed p).
first_step: Check whether 'N𝔞 for 𝔞 | (p+2c√−d)' with c,d in boxes is an incomplete-norm-form set in Maynard's sense.
refs: Maynard, Primes represented by incomplete norm forms, arXiv:1507.05080

title: Maynard primes with restricted digits → thin sets with Fourier control
connection: Maynard (Invent. 2019) counts primes with a missing decimal digit by strong Fourier bounds on the thin digit set; the set of ES-hard residue patterns (Mordell classes mod 840 and deeper digit-like conditions mod 4C) is a digit-like thin set.
why: Template for proving that a thin, Fourier-structured set of p's must intersect the ES-good set.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform (mod M = 840·k) of the indicator of 'not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M' and compare its L1 norm with Maynard's digit-set bounds.
refs: Maynard, Primes with restricted digits, Invent. Math. 217 (2019), arXiv:1604.01041

title: Merikoski largest prime factor of n²+1 → ES Type I values p²+4c²d
connection: Merikoski (JEMS 2023) shows P⁺(n²+1) > n^{1.279} using Deshouillers–Iwaniec Kloosterman bounds on divisors of n²+1 in ranges; ES Type I needs a divisor of p²+4c²d in a specific class and range.
why: His divisor-in-range distribution for quadratic values is the closest existing tool to 'a divisor of a quadratic value lies in a prescribed window'.
first_step: Re-derive Merikoski's Type I/II information for the polynomial X² + 4c²d (X = p fixed, c varying) and record the admissible divisor ranges.
refs: Merikoski, Largest prime factor of n^2+1, arXiv:1908.08816

title: de la Bretèche–Drappeau level of distribution of quadratic polynomials
connection: de la Bretèche–Drappeau (JEMS 2020) prove level of distribution beyond 1 for #{n ≤ x : q | n² + D} averaged over q; ES Type I is 'f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd)'.
why: Exactly the object (divisors of a quadratic value) with level > 1 — needed when f is larger than the square root.
first_step: Check whether their result allows a residue condition f ≡ a (mod 4cd) on the modulus f itself, and whether the polynomial variable can be c (with p fixed).
refs: de la Bretèche–Drappeau, Niveau de répartition des polynômes quadratiques et crible majorant pour les entiers friables, JEMS 22 (2020)

title: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec / Tóth equidistribution of roots of quadratic congruences with modulus condition
connection: Roots ν/f of ν² ≡ −D (mod f) equidistribute (DFI 1995 primes, Tóth composite); ES Type I asks that p be such a root (p² ≡ −4c²d mod f) while f ≡ −p mod 4cd — a joint condition on root and modulus.
why: Joint equidistribution of (root mod f, f mod m) pairs is a natural theorem to aim for and would give averaged Type I counts in new ranges.
first_step: Compute empirically, for D = 4c²d fixed small and f ≤ 10^6, the joint distribution of (ν/f, f mod 4cd) and check for correlation.
refs: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec, Equidistribution of roots of a quadratic congruence to prime moduli, Ann. Math. 141 (1995)

title: Dunn–Kerr–Shparlinski–Zaharescu bilinear forms with modular square roots
connection: DKSZ bound bilinear sums Σ α_m β_n e(h√(mn)/q) over modular square roots; ES Type I at fixed f involves √(−4c²d) mod f, bilinear in (c, d).
why: Bilinear square-root sums are exactly what appears when one Fourier-expands the Type I condition in c and d.
first_step: Fourier-expand 1_{p² ≡ −4c²d (mod f)} and isolate the bilinear square-root sum; compare with DKSZ hypotheses.
refs: Dunn–Kerr–Shparlinski–Zaharescu, Bilinear forms in Weyl sums for modular square roots and applications, arXiv:1908.10143

title: Kowalski–Michel–Sawin bilinear forms with Kloosterman sums
connection: KMS (Annals 2017) beat Pólya–Vinogradov for bilinear sums of Kloosterman sums in short ranges; ES Type II ff′ = 1 + 4c²dp is a modular hyperbola whose counting leads to Kloosterman sums with modulus tied to (c,d,p).
why: Short-range Kloosterman bilinear bounds are needed precisely because ES moduli 4cd are small relative to the hyperbola size.
first_step: Expand the Type II count for fixed (c,d) into Kloosterman sums S(h, ·; 4cd) and check whether the (c,d)-average is a KMS bilinear form.
refs: Kowalski–Michel–Sawin, Bilinear forms with Kloosterman sums and applications, Ann. Math. 186 (2017), arXiv:1511.01636

title: Bettin–Chandee trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions
connection: Bettin–Chandee bound Σ α_m β_n ν_a e(a·m̄/n); ES exponential sums carry e(h·\overline{4c}/p) or e(h·p̄/4c) fractions with three free variables (h, c, d).
why: Trilinear structure matches the three ES certificate parameters.
first_step: Write the Type I/II indicator's Fourier expansion, identify the trilinear Kloosterman-fraction sum, and check BC's ranges.
refs: Bettin–Chandee, Trilinear forms with Kloosterman fractions, arXiv:1502.00769

title: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel trace functions over primes for ES residue indicators
connection: FKM show algebraic trace functions K(n) mod q have Σ_{p≤x} K(p) = o(π(x)) for x ≥ q^{3/4+ε}; ES conditions like '(−p mod 4C) ∈ some set' are trace-function-type functions of p.
why: Gives equidistribution of primes p against arbitrary algebraic weights — e.g. the set of p for which a given finite menu fails mod q.
first_step: Check whether the 'menu failure' indicator mod a prime q (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS.md) is a bounded-conductor trace function and apply FKM to get prime densities.
refs: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel, Algebraic trace functions over the primes, Duke Math. J. 163 (2014)

title: Polymath8 Type III / Deligne estimates for τ3-like ES counts
connection: Polymath8a's Type III estimates use Deligne's RH for correlations of hyper-Kloosterman sums to put τ3 in APs beyond 1/2; ES Type II solution counts are restricted triple-divisor counts (three denominators).
why: τ3-in-APs technology is the natural input for counting ES solutions in APs of n.
first_step: Write f(n) restricted to a fixed residue class of n as a τ3-type sum and test what level of distribution in n the ET average proof needs.
refs: Polymath, New equidistribution estimates of Zhang type, Algebra & Number Theory 8 (2014)

title: Irving / Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang divisor function in APs to smooth or prime-power moduli
connection: Irving (2015) and Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang get τ(n) equidistributed in APs to smooth / prime-power moduli beyond 2/3; ES's tied modulus 4C can be chosen a power of 2 times smooth.
why: Choosing 4C = 2^k is a legitimate ES sub-family (TWO_POWER_LADDER) and prime-power moduli have extra equidistribution.
first_step: Compare TWO_POWER_LADDER.md counts with the divisor-in-AP-to-2^k asymptotic; check which range of k the LSZ theorem covers.
refs: Irving, The divisor function in arithmetic progressions to smooth moduli, IMRN 2015
Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang, Divisor problem in arithmetic progressions modulo a prime power, Adv. Math. (2018)

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for 'no divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C)'
connection: For C = 1, 'N has no divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)' iff all odd prime factors of N are ≡ 1 (mod 4): a half-dimensional sifted set (Landau–Ramanujan). For general C, ES failure at N requires the prime factors of N to avoid generating −1 in (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: The semi-linear sieve gives sharp upper and lower bounds for such sifted sets; summing over C at fixed p could bound the failure probability.
first_step: For fixed p, compute #{C ≤ X : 4Cp+1 has no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C} and compare with the semi-linear sieve prediction ∏(1 − 1/ℓ)^{1/2}-type density.
refs: Iwaniec, Rosser's sieve, Acta Arith. 36 (1980)
Friedlander–Iwaniec, Opera de Cribro (2010)

title: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki 'when the sieve works'
connection: GKM (Duke 2015) characterise when sifted sets by a set of primes have the expected density; the 'divisors avoid a coset structure' condition in ES is a sifted-set condition on prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Precise conditions for sieve heuristics to be correct are what a pointwise lower-tail claim needs.
first_step: Check whether the sifting set 'primes ℓ whose class mod 4C lies in a subgroup H not containing −1' satisfies GKM hypotheses uniformly in C.
refs: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki, When the sieve works, Duke Math. J. 164 (2015)

title: Ford–Maynard theory of prime-producing sieves
connection: Ford–Maynard analyse which sieve-theoretic information (Type I/II ranges) can and cannot produce primes, extending the parity problem; ES is a 'one witness among polylog' problem with a parity-like barrier.
why: A formal limit theory for sieve information could make the campaign's B-barriers precise or show a gap.
first_step: Check whether Ford–Maynard's framework (arXiv 2024) includes sequences where the target is 'has a divisor in a class' rather than 'is prime'.
refs: Ford–Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368

title: Koukoulopoulos–Tao / Ford–Koukoulopoulos–Tao Erdős–Hooley Δ for residue classes
connection: KT and FKT determine the mean of Hooley's Δ(n) = max_u #{d | n : u < d ≤ eu} up to (log log)^{O(1)}; ES needs concentration of divisors of N in a residue class (−1 mod 4C) rather than in a dyadic interval.
why: A 'Δ for residue classes' — max over classes mod m of #{d | N : d ≡ a} — is the ES-native concentration function and its distribution methods (random walks on divisors) may transfer.
first_step: Define Δ_m(N) = max_a #{d|N : d ≡ a mod m} and compute its distribution for N = 4Cp+1 vs random N; read the FKT lower-bound construction.
refs: Koukoulopoulos–Tao, An upper bound on the mean value of the Erdős–Hooley Delta function, arXiv:2306.08615
Ford–Koukoulopoulos–Tao, A lower bound on the mean value of the Erdős–Hooley Delta function, arXiv:2308.11987

title: Ford's divisors-in-intervals H(x,y,2y) method for divisors in residue classes
connection: Ford (Annals 2008) determined the order of #{n ≤ x : n has a divisor in (y,2y]} with a (log)^{−δ}(loglog)^{−3/2} factor; ES needs a divisor in a residue class mod 4C, and the analogous 'has a divisor in class' count.
why: Ford's structure (anatomy, entropy of divisor sets) predicts the shape of the ES lower tail and its failure modes.
first_step: Formulate H_m(x) = #{n ≤ x : n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m with d ≤ √n} and compute it for m = 4C, C ≤ 50, x = 10^8; compare with Ford-type heuristics.
refs: Ford, The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval, Ann. Math. 168 (2008)

title: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum arcsine law in residue classes
connection: DDT: log d / log n for a random divisor d | n has the arcsine law on average; ES needs divisors d of N in a narrow size window and a residue class.
why: Joint (size, class) distribution of random divisors controls how many ES certificates exist.
first_step: Compute the joint distribution of (log d/log N, d mod 4C) for N = 4Cp+1 and check independence numerically.
refs: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum, Lois de répartition des diviseurs, Acta Arith. 34 (1979)

title: Erdős primitive-set / Lichtman: ES-covered n as a set of multiples
connection: Since a solution for n gives one for every multiple of n, the set of n covered by any fixed family of identities is a set of multiples ℳ(B) of a primitive set B; Lichtman (2022) proved the Erdős primitive set conjecture Σ 1/(b log b) ≤ Σ_p 1/(p log p).
why: Sets-of-multiples theory (Besicovitch, Erdős, Hall) quantifies how much a family covers and how the uncovered set (divisor-closed) can look.
first_step: For the repo's identity menus up to modulus M, compute the primitive generator set B among primes ≤ 10^7 and the density of ℳ(B); test whether Σ_{b∈B} 1/(b log b) tracks the uncovered density.
refs: Lichtman, A proof of the Erdős primitive set conjecture, arXiv:2202.02384
Hall, Sets of Multiples (CUP 1996)

title: Banks–Ford–Tao: probabilistic prime models fail → refine the ES zero law
connection: BFT (Invent. 2023) show Cramér-type random models of primes mispredict large gaps and propose corrected models; the campaign's (J)97 lottery zero law for ES failures is a random model of the same kind.
why: Siblings fail less than the zero law predicts (G4); a BFT-style correction (sieving by small primes first) could explain it.
first_step: Rebuild the ES lottery model with residue-class sieving by primes ≤ z (BFT 'Granville model') and refit to S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failure data.
refs: Banks–Ford–Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, arXiv:1908.08613

title: Harper random multiplicative functions: lower-tail of divisor-character sums
connection: Harper proved better-than-square-root cancellation for low moments of random multiplicative function sums (Forum Pi 2020) via multiplicative chaos; ES counts R(p) are sums over divisors of p-tied integers twisted by characters mod 4C.
why: Multiplicative chaos is the known mechanism for unusual lower tails of divisor-structured sums.
first_step: Model R(p) as Σ_C Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} 1_{d≡−1 (4C)} with prime factorizations randomized, and compute its lower-tail exponent by simulation vs Harper-type predictions.
refs: Harper, Moments of random multiplicative functions, I: low moments, better than squareroot cancellation, and critical multiplicative chaos, arXiv:1703.06654

title: Kozma–Samotij lower tails via relative entropy for R(p)
connection: Kozma–Samotij prove lower-tail large deviations for subgraph counts via relative entropy; R(p) is a count of 'arithmetic subgraphs' (divisor relations) in a random-like structure.
why: ES's core difficulty is the one-sided lower tail R(p) ≥ ε·M_BM(p); entropy methods are the modern lower-tail tool.
first_step: Map the ES certificate count to a polynomial in independent-ish Bernoulli variables (ℓ | 4Cp+1) and check the KS hypotheses (bounded influence) on data.
refs: Kozma–Samotij, Lower tails via relative entropy, arXiv:2104.04850

title: Harel–Mousset–Samotij upper tails via entropic stability (dual for R(p))
connection: HMS 'Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability' gives sharp upper tails for subgraph counts; for ES, upper-tail control of the *failure* indicator counts translates into exceptional-set bounds.
why: Exceptional-set results are upper tails of a 'number of uncovered p' variable.
first_step: Write E(N) as a polynomial count and check whether HMS-type moment methods give anything beyond Vaughan-type bounds.
refs: Harel–Mousset–Samotij, Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability, Duke Math. J. (2022), arXiv:1904.08212

title: Janson/Suen inequality with modern dependency graphs for 'no certificate' event
connection: Janson's inequality bounds P(no event) ≤ exp(−μ + Δ/2) for monotone events; 'no ES certificate at p' is an intersection of complements of divisor events.
why: μ ≍ log²p so exp(−μ) is tiny; the issue is Δ (correlations). Modern refinements (Riordan–Warnke) handle non-monotone dependencies.
first_step: Compute μ and Δ empirically for a hard prime; test Riordan–Warnke's 'Janson inequality for general events' conditions.
refs: Riordan–Warnke, The Janson inequalities for general up-sets, Random Struct. Alg. 46 (2015)

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for the ES certificate count
connection: Stein's method bounds total-variation distance of a count to Poisson; if R(p) were approximately Poisson(μ) with μ ≍ log²p, P(R=0) ≈ e^{−μ}.
why: Gives a quantitative heuristic and identifies which dependencies (shared prime factors) break Poisson behaviour.
first_step: Compute the Arratia–Goldstein–Gordon b1,b2,b3 terms for the ES certificate events at p ≤ 10^6 on data.
refs: Arratia–Goldstein–Gordon, Two moments suffice for Poisson approximations, Ann. Prob. 17 (1989)

title: Granville–Soundararajan pretentiousness of the 'class of divisors' character
connection: Pretentious theory: a multiplicative function f is small on average unless it pretends to be n^{it}χ(n); the indicator of 'N has a divisor in class −1 mod m' expands via characters χ mod m into Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|N} χ(d).
why: The ES failure set is where all such character divisor sums conspire; pretentious distance gives a language for 'conspiracy'.
first_step: For each failing N (no divisor ≡ −1 mod m), compute the pretentious distance D(χ_m-twisted divisor sums) and see whether failures cluster at a pretentious character (e.g. the real character mod m).

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD-graph compression (Duffin–Schaeffer)
connection: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard proved Duffin–Schaeffer (Annals 2020) by a compression argument on GCD graphs controlling overlaps between rational approximations a/q; ES is a question about approximating 4/n by short Egyptian sums, with overlap structure between certificates sharing common factors.

connection: Petrow–Young (Annals 2020) prove the Weyl-strength subconvex bound L(1/2,χ) ≪ q^{1/6+ε} for all Dirichlet χ; ES counts expand over characters mod 4C.

connection: Kelley–Meka get quasi-polynomial bounds for 3-AP-free sets via almost-periodicity + spectral positivity; the ES e-slice asks whether −1 lies in the quotient set Q = {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} ⊂ (ℤ/e)^×, an additive-combinatorial (multiplicative-group) statement.

title: Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa (Gowers–Green–Manners–Tao) for divisor quotient sets
connection: PFR (Marton) over 𝔽₂ⁿ and torsion-free groups: small doubling ⇒ covered by few cosets of a subgroup; the set of prime factors of N mod e generates the ES quotient set.

title: Balandraud's sharp subset-sum theorem in ℤ/p for the 'target −1' problem
connection: Balandraud: subset sums of k distinct nonzero residues mod a prime cover ≥ min(p, k(k+1)/2+1) elements; taking discrete logs, ES's subset-products of prime factors of N in (ℤ/e)^× is a subset-sum problem in ℤ/(e−1).

connection: For prime e, −1 ∈ H ⊂ 𝔽_e^× iff |H| is even; the e-slice needs −1 in the quotient set Q (not the generated subgroup), but −1 ∈ ⟨Q⟩ is a necessary condition expressed via 2-adic valuations of multiplicative orders.

refs: Moree, Artin's primitive root conjecture – a survey, arXiv:math/0412262

connection: Bourgain's sum-product and exponential-sum bounds for arbitrary q handle composite moduli; ES moduli 4C, 4cd are composite and smooth.

connection: Huang's proof uses a signed adjacency matrix of the hypercube and Cauchy interlacing to force a high-degree vertex in any large induced subgraph; ES certificates live on a product of small 'choice' cubes (choice of prime factors into a,b).

title: Pila–Wilkie / Binyamini–Novikov sharply o-minimal counting for ES real-analytic families
connection: Pila–Wilkie counts rational points on transcendental parts of definable sets; Binyamini–Novikov(–Zack) give effective polylog versions for sharply o-minimal structures. ES counting functions involve log-like main terms in a definable family (the real points of U_n as n varies).
why: The count M_BM(p) ≍ log² p is polylogarithmic — the same scale as sharply o-minimal point counts; a structural explanation of 'polylog' could come from there.
first_step: Check whether the set {(n, x/n, y/n, z/n)} is definable in ℝ_exp after a log-scaling and whether its algebraic part is all of it (then Pila–Wilkie says nothing).
refs: Binyamini–Novikov–Zack, Sharply o-minimal structures and sharp cellular decomposition, arXiv:2209.10972
Pila–Wilkie, The rational points of a definable set, Duke Math. J. 133 (2006)

title: Uniform dimension growth (Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen) for upper bounds on f(n)
connection: CCDN prove uniform polynomial-in-degree bounds for rational points of bounded height on projective varieties (determinant method); f(n) is a count of integral points of bounded height on U_n.
why: Uniform upper bounds f(n) ≪ n^ε are inputs for second-moment/variance arguments.
first_step: Compare the CCDN bound applied to U_n with the trivial divisor bound f(n) ≪ n^{ε}; see whether it gives anything uniform in a range of heights.
refs: Castryck–Cluckers–Dittmann–Nguyen, The dimension growth conjecture, polynomial in the degree and without logarithmic factors, arXiv:1904.13109

title: Corvaja–Zannier degeneracy of integral points via the subspace theorem
connection: CZ (Annals 2004) prove non-density of integral points on affine surfaces whose boundary has many components; U_n's boundary has 3 lines (log CY), the borderline case where integral points may be dense.
why: Adding extra boundary (e.g. requiring x,y,z to avoid primes in a set S, i.e. S-integral constraints) pushes into the CZ degenerate regime — giving finiteness of 'too-structured' solution families.
first_step: Determine the number of boundary components needed for CZ when imposing 'xyz is S-smooth' and deduce a finiteness lemma for S-smooth ES solutions across n.
refs: Corvaja–Zannier, On integral points on surfaces, Ann. Math. 160 (2004)

title: S-unit equation finiteness: ES solutions with all denominators S-smooth
connection: If x, y, z, n are all S-units for a fixed finite set S, then 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is an S-unit equation with finitely many non-degenerate solutions (Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt).
why: Gives a rigorous negative: no fixed finite set of primes can supply the denominators for infinitely many primes n — a clean barrier for 'smooth-denominator' constructions.
first_step: Write the S-unit equation and its explicit Evertse bound; compare with the data on smoothness of ES denominators at p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt, Linear equations in variables which lie in a multiplicative group, Ann. Math. 155 (2002)

title: Chabauty–Kim / quadratic Chabauty on ES-derived S-unit curves
connection: Chabauty–Kim computes integral points on P¹ − {0,1,∞} (S-unit equations) and higher-genus curves (Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk); ES-derived S-unit curves appear when two denominators are constrained to be S-units.
why: Explicit computation of the finitely many exceptions would turn the S-unit barrier into data.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, compute all solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z with x,y,z,n S-units by brute force / known S-unit solvers.
refs: Balakrishnan–Dogra–Müller–Tuitman–Vonk, Explicit Chabauty–Kim for the split Cartan modular curve of level 13, Ann. Math. 189 (2019)

title: Universal torsors of the Cayley cubic for parametrising ES solutions
connection: Integral points on singular del Pezzo surfaces are parametrised via universal torsors (Derenthal, Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc); the Type I/II divisor forms are presumably the torsor equations of U_n.
why: A torsor parametrisation makes integral points into lattice points with coprimality — the setting for geometry-of-numbers and circle-method counts.
first_step: Compute the Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic (blow-up of P² in 6 points of a complete quadrilateral) and write the torsor equation with the ES boundary.
refs: Derenthal, Singular del Pezzo surfaces whose universal torsors are hypersurfaces, Proc. LMS 108 (2014)

title: Santens / Wilsch integral Manin conjecture applied to U_n
connection: Santens proves Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties; Wilsch counts integral points on log Fano threefolds; Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel give the predicted shape. f(n) is a count of integral points on the log CY U_n (not log Fano) with growing n.
why: The log CY case predicts polylog growth — matching M_BM ≍ log²; an integral-Manin framework could give a conceptual main term.
first_step: Compute Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel's predicted exponent of log B for integral points on the Cayley cubic minus triangle and compare with log² p.
refs: Santens, Manin's conjecture for integral points on toric varieties, arXiv:2312.13914
Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold, arXiv:1901.08503

title: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin: Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces
connection: BLS prove HP for 100% of Fano hypersurfaces of fixed degree and dimension ordered by height; ES gives a one-parameter family (in n), not a random family.
why: Calibrates: one-parameter families are exactly where 'random family' methods do not apply.
first_step: Record the family dimension needed in BLS's argument and compare with the ES family {U_n} (dimension 1).
refs: Browning–Le Boudec–Sawin, The Hasse principle for random Fano hypersurfaces, Ann. Math. 197 (2023), arXiv:2006.02356

title: Sections of the ES fibration over 𝔽_q(t) via free rational curves (Browning–Sawin)
connection: Browning–Sawin use the function-field circle method to count/describe spaces of rational curves on hypersurfaces; ES polynomial identities are sections of U → A¹_n, i.e. rational curves on the total space.
why: Counting sections of bounded degree over 𝔽_q(t) quantifies the Mordell–Schinzel barrier and might find all identity families of a given degree.
first_step: Set up the moduli of degree-d sections of the ES total space over 𝔽_q(t) and compute its dimension; compare with known Mordell/Schinzel identity families.
refs: Browning–Sawin, Free rational curves on low degree hypersurfaces and the circle method, arXiv:1810.06882

title: Graber–Harris–Starr sections exist over ℂ(t): why identities exist geometrically but not integrally
connection: GHS: rationally connected fibrations over curves have sections; U → A¹_n has rational fibres, so sections exist over ℂ(n) and ℚ(n) (identities with rational denominators), but Mordell–Schinzel shows none integral covering square classes.
why: Makes the integrality defect precise: it's an 'integral section' problem, whose obstructions are at the special fibres (n = square).
first_step: Compute the degenerate fibres of the integral model over Spec ℤ[n] and interpret the Mordell–Schinzel barrier as nonexistence of integral sections through specific fibre components.
refs: Graber–Harris–Starr, Families of rationally connected varieties, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Bhargava–Gauss composition of x²+4dy² values in Type I
connection: Type I needs f | p² + 4c²d: values of the form X² + 4dY² at (p,c); divisors of represented values are represented by forms in the same genus/class group (composition).
why: Recasts the Type I event as a class-group statement about the ideal above f in the order of discriminant −16d — where Bhargava cubes / composition laws act.
first_step: For hard primes, compute the class-group element of each prime divisor of p²+4c²d and see whether the failure is explained by class-group parity.
refs: Bhargava, Higher composition laws I, Ann. Math. 159 (2004)

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland homological stability & Cohen–Lenstra over 𝔽_q(t)
connection: EVW prove Cohen–Lenstra-type statistics over function fields via homological stability of Hurwitz spaces; ES over 𝔽_q[T] has proved variants and class-group input in its Type I.
why: Class-group distribution in the function-field ES certificate families could be computed exactly via Hurwitz-space methods.
first_step: Identify which class groups (of 𝔽_q[T][√(−D(T))]) enter the function-field ES Type I and check whether EVW-type results give their 2-parts.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh–Westerland, Homological stability for Hurwitz spaces and the Cohen–Lenstra conjecture over function fields, Ann. Math. 183 (2016)

title: Landesman–Levy Cohen–Lenstra moments over function fields via stable homology
connection: Landesman–Levy (2024) prove the Cohen–Lenstra moments over 𝔽_q(t) (for q large relative to the moment) via the stable homology of non-splitting Hurwitz spaces; function-field ES is a natural test bed for such random-model predictions.
why: Large-q limits often make 'every n' statements provable (Lang–Weil); here they could validate the ES random-model zero law in a sibling.
first_step: Formulate the function-field ES lower-tail statement as a point count on a Hurwitz-type space and check whether stability arguments apply.
refs: Landesman–Levy, The Cohen–Lenstra moments over function fields via the stable homology of non-splitting Hurwitz spaces, arXiv:2410.22210

title: Smith's Rédei-symbol / governing-field method for distributions of 'sterility' across p
connection: A. Smith's work on 2^∞-Selmer and class groups uses governing fields and additive combinatorics on Boolean cubes of twists to get distributions of higher Rédei symbols; ES T1 is a reciprocity (Rédei-type) obstruction and repo memos treat Rédei matrices.
why: Could prove that 'sterility patterns' up to depth k have the predicted distribution across p — a structured 100%-type statement.
first_step: Model ES sterility at depth k (fixed moduli) as a Rédei-matrix event and compute its distribution over p ≤ 10^8; compare with a Smith-type uniform model.
refs: Smith, The distribution of ℓ^∞-Selmer groups in degree ℓ twist families I, arXiv:2207.05674

title: Koymans–Pagano Stevenhagen conjecture (negative Pell) — '−1 as a target' analogy
connection: Koymans–Pagano proved Stevenhagen's conjecture on the density of D for which x² − Dy² = −1 is solvable; negative Pell asks whether −1 is a norm of a unit, ES's B2 asks whether −1 lies in the divisor quotient set.
why: Both are '−1 hitting' problems whose obstructions are 2-adic/Rédei; the negative-Pell proof technology handles exactly the −1 target.
first_step: Write the e-slice event for e prime as 'class of −1 in a ray class group generated by primes dividing N' and compare with the negative-Pell 4-rank/8-rank framework.
refs: Koymans–Pagano, On Stevenhagen's conjecture, arXiv:2201.13424

title: Chan–Koymans–Milovic–Pagano negative Pell lower bounds via 8-rank
connection: CKMP get the lower bound side of negative Pell densities via 8-ranks; template for proving lower bounds for '−1 attained' events.
why: ES needs a lower-bound (existence) statement — the side negative-Pell work had to prove separately.
first_step: Read the CKMP argument and identify the step converting 'distribution of ranks' into 'at least this proportion attain −1'.
refs: Chan–Koymans–Milovic–Pagano, On the negative Pell equation, arXiv:1908.01752

title: Pierce et al. ℓ-torsion & Ellenberg–Venkatesh lemma: many small split primes ⇒ small torsion
connection: The EV lemma converts many small split primes into ℓ-torsion bounds; ES Type I needs small split primes in Q(√−d) in specific classes.
why: Reverse direction: class-group structure (small 2-torsion) forces many small primes in many classes, possibly including the ES-needed class.
first_step: For d ≤ 100 and hard p, compute the classes of small split primes in Cl(−16d) and whether the Type I-needed class is hit.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh, Reflection principles and bounds for class group torsion, IMRN 2007

title: Mordell–Weil / elliptic fibrations on the Cayley cubic resolution
connection: The minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic is a weak del Pezzo of degree 3; pencils of anticanonical sections give elliptic fibrations whose fibres carry group laws.
why: Group laws on fibres could produce new ES solutions from old (chord–tangent) with integrality tracked — a source of solution-generating operations.
first_step: Pick a pencil of plane sections through a node, compute the elliptic fibration, and test whether adding a torsion section maps integral ES points to integral ES points.
refs: BRAINSTORM/elliptic_fibration_es.md

title: Cremona symmetries of the Cayley cubic and ES solution moves
connection: The Cayley cubic's automorphism/birational symmetry group includes S₄ on the nodes and quadratic Cremona maps (inversion x ↦ 1/x relates to the reciprocal plane); ES only uses S₃ permutations.
why: Any extra symmetry preserving the integral structure would give the missing ES 'group action' (cf. Chen/Markoff).
first_step: List the birational automorphisms of σ₃ = 0 commuting with w′ = const and test their action on ES solutions for small n.
refs: BRAINSTORM/cayley_markoff_cm.md

title: Igusa / Denef–Loeser uniform p-adic integration for local densities of U_n
connection: Uniform p-adic integration (Cluckers–Loeser motivic integration) computes local densities σ_ℓ(n) uniformly in ℓ and n; the ES main term M_BM is an Euler product of such densities.
why: Uniformity in n of local densities is needed for any pointwise main-term statement.
first_step: Compute σ_ℓ(n) symbolically for the Cayley-cubic model and check uniformity across n mod ℓ^k.
refs: Cluckers–Loeser, Constructible motivic functions and motivic integration, Invent. Math. 173 (2008)

title: Perfectoid tilting Q_p(p^{1/p^∞}) ↔ 𝔽_p((t^{1/p^∞})) for local ES statements (honest low-value item)
connection: Scholze's tilting equivalence relates étale covers in mixed and equal characteristic; ES over 𝔽_q[T] has proved variants, but tilting is a local (p-adic) statement and ES's difficulty is global.
why: Recorded for completeness: the only ES-side objects it can touch are local solubility and local densities, which are already known.
first_step: Check whether any repo statement uses a local-at-p fact over 𝔽_q((t)) that lacks a mixed-characteristic counterpart; if none, close this item.

title: Condensed/analytic-stack adelic formalism for the integral BM set (honest low-value item)
connection: Clausen–Scholze condensed mathematics gives a uniform framework for topological algebra over all places; the integral Brauer–Manin set of U_n is an adelic topological object.
why: Only a formalism; possibly useful for a clean statement of 'non-BM integral HP failure' families, not for existence.
first_step: Check whether a condensed formulation changes anything in BL's computation; most likely not — record and close.
refs: Clausen–Scholze, Lectures on condensed mathematics (2019)

title: Fargues–Scholze / local Langlands — no natural ES object (recorded)
connection: Geometrisation of local Langlands (Fargues–Scholze) concerns representations of p-adic groups; ES has no evident reductive-group or Galois-representation object attached.
why: Recording the null result prevents later re-proposal; the nearest real link would go through automorphic forms attached to ES counts (theta series), which are GL₂/GL₁ and need no geometrisation.
first_step: Ask whether any ES count is a Fourier coefficient of an automorphic form on a group of rank ≥ 2; if not, close.
refs: Fargues–Scholze, Geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence, arXiv:2102.13459

title: Geometric Langlands over function fields (Gaitsgory et al.; OAI 014) for function-field ES counts
connection: Over 𝔽_q(t), Hecke eigensheaves geometrise automorphic forms; function-field ES counts are point counts on varieties over 𝔽_q whose cohomology might be automorphic.
why: Function-field ES has proved variants; a sheaf-theoretic count could give exact formulas for solution numbers in degree d.

title: Motivic / Grothendieck-ring class of U_n and its point counts
connection: The class [U_n] in K₀(Var) and its point counts #U_n(𝔽_ℓ) are computable (Cayley cubic minus triangle); integral-point main terms are built from such local counts.
why: Exact point counts mod ℓ give exact local densities and identify any 'local sterility' structure for free.

title: Integral points on hyperplane-arrangement complements (very affine varieties) via tropical compactification
connection: The torus part of U_n (all coordinates nonzero) is P² minus 4 lines in reciprocal coordinates — a very affine variety; tropical compactifications (Tevelev) and Huh's likelihood geometry study such varieties.
why: Tropicalisation shows which valuation patterns (sizes of x,y,z relative to n) integral points can have — a size-pattern classification of ES solutions.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety of the reciprocal plane and compare its cones with the observed (log x, log y, log z)/log n patterns of ES solutions at p ≤ 10^6.
refs: Tevelev, Compactifications of subvarieties of tori, Amer. J. Math. 129 (2007)
Huh, The maximum likelihood degree of a very affine variety, Compositio 149 (2013)

title: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang polynomially effective unipotent equidistribution
connection: LMW (2022) give polynomially effective equidistribution for one-parameter unipotent orbits in SL₂(ℝ)×SL₂(ℝ)/Γ and SL₂(ℂ)/Γ-type spaces; ES Type II solutions are SL₂(ℤ) matrices [[f,a],[b,f′]] with ab = 4c²dp and f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd), i.e. lattice points in a thin region of SL₂.
why: Effective rates are the prerequisite for counting lattice points in shrinking/thin regions (polylog many expected).
first_step: Write the Type II count as a count of Γ₀(4cd)-points in a region of SL₂(ℝ) depending on p and estimate its volume vs LMW error terms.
refs: Lindenstrauss–Mohammadi–Wang, Effective equidistribution for some one parameter unipotent flows, arXiv:2211.11099

title: Type II as SL₂(ℤ) matrices with prescribed off-diagonal product (hyperbolic lattice counting)
connection: ff′ − ab = 1 with ab = 4c²dp: Type II certificates are integer matrices of determinant 1 with diagonal ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) and off-diagonal product fixed — a hyperbolic lattice-point problem in Γ(4cd)-cosets.
why: Spectral counting in congruence subgroups (Selberg 3/16, Kim–Sarnak 7/64) applies; the fixed product ab is a 'divisor-split' constraint.
first_step: Count matrices in a coset of Γ(4cd) with |entries| ≤ T and ab = 4c²dp numerically, compare with the spectral main term.
refs: Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms (2002)
Kim–Sarnak, appendix to Kim, Functoriality for the exterior square of GL4…, JAMS 16 (2003)

title: Einsiedler–Margulis–(Mohammadi–)Venkatesh effective equidistribution of closed semisimple orbits
connection: EMV/EMMV give effective equidistribution of closed orbits of semisimple groups (e.g. SO(Q) for ternary Q) with polynomial rates; ES has ternary-form and quaternion reformulations.
why: Closed-orbit equidistribution yields local-global for representations of large integers by forms — with effective rates, potentially of a whole genus.
first_step: Pick the repo's ternary/quaternion ES reformulation (QUATERNION_ES.md) and identify the closed orbit whose equidistribution would give the needed representations.

title: Ellenberg–Michel–Venkatesh: Linnik's ergodic method with a split-prime condition
connection: EMV prove equidistribution of integer points on spheres (and representations of lattices) assuming a fixed prime splits — Linnik's condition; ES-related ternary representations have exactly this kind of auxiliary prime condition.
why: Linnik's method gives results at individual large integers, not on average — the pointwise shape ES needs — at the cost of a splitting condition.

title: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira joint equidistribution of integer points and their orthogonal lattices
connection: AES prove joint equidistribution of primitive integer points on spheres together with the shape of their orthogonal lattice; ES certificates carry both a 'point' (solution) and an associated lattice (L_ρ).
why: Joint equidistribution could say the ES-relevant lattice shape is generic, so short vectors in cones (ES) exist for most representations.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice L_ρ at p as the orthogonal lattice of a vector and check whether AES's setup matches.

connection: Duke's theorem: class-group orbits (CM points, closed geodesics) equidistribute as discriminant → ∞; OAI 015 claims higher-degree torus-packet equidistribution. ES Type I lives in class groups of discriminant −16d tied to p.
why: Equidistribution of class-group packets is a pointwise-in-discriminant statement — at one discriminant, all of the packet equidistributes.

title: Duke–Schulze-Pillot: large integers represented by ternary forms outside spinor exceptions
connection: Every sufficiently large integer (with bounded divisibility at anisotropic primes) locally represented by a positive ternary form's spinor genus is represented by the form (ineffective); ES reformulations via ternary forms would inherit this.
why: This is the classical tool that converts local solubility into global representability pointwise for large n — exactly ES's shape.

title: Spinor exceptions as the analogue of T1
connection: Ternary forms fail to represent certain integers t·m² (spinor exceptional square classes) despite local solubility; ES Type I/II fails at odd squares m² despite local solubility (T1).
why: Both are square-class obstructions in a local-global problem; the spinor-exception theory (Schulze-Pillot, Earnest–Hsia) has a precise algebraic explanation that might map to T1.

title: Blomer–Harcos hybrid subconvexity for effective ternary representations
connection: Blomer–Harcos give hybrid subconvexity for twisted L-functions, enabling effective representation results for ternary forms (with Siegel caveats); ES's ternary analogues would need such input.
why: Effective bounds combined with 10^18 verification are the only way a ternary route could close a range.
first_step: Quantify the size beyond which Blomer–Harcos yields representations, for the discriminants arising in any ES ternary reformulation.
refs: Blomer–Harcos, Hybrid bounds for twisted L-functions, J. reine angew. Math. 621 (2008)

title: Bhargava–Hanke 290 / Rouse 451: finite-check universality as a template
connection: Bhargava–Hanke show a positive integral quadratic form is universal iff it represents 29 specific integers ≤ 290; Rouse's 451-theorem (odds) is conditional on GRH. ES is a 'universal representation' statement with a cubic form.
why: Finite-check theorems for universality rely on escalation + ternary sub-lattice theory; an 'escalator' for ES identity families could be explored.

refs: Bhargava–Hanke, Universal quadratic forms and the 290-Theorem (preprint)

title: Kudla programme / arithmetic Siegel–Weil (Li–Zhang Kudla–Rapoport) for ES theta quotients
connection: Kudla's programme relates generating series of special cycles to derivatives of Eisenstein series; Li–Zhang proved the Kudla–Rapoport conjecture. ES has theta-quotient reformulations (KUDLA_ES.md).
why: Arithmetic intersection numbers equal Fourier coefficients of derivatives — an exact identity; positivity of intersection numbers could force positivity of counts.
first_step: Identify which ES count, if any, appears as a degree of a special cycle (positive by geometry), per KUDLA_ES.md.

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth cycle integrals for ES₅ geodesic data
connection: DIT express traces of modular functions over closed geodesics (indefinite forms) as coefficients of mock modular forms; ES₅/CF-length data is geodesic (Hirzebruch–Jung, Dedekind) data of rationals tied to p.
why: A mock-modular generating function for CF-statistics could encode ES₅ counts with exact modular transformation laws.

connection: Ghys: linking numbers of modular knots with the trefoil equal the Rademacher function of the hyperbolic matrix; ES₅ words are SL₂(ℤ) matrices whose CF structure is short.

connection: Shifted convolution sums Σ a(n)b(n+h) of automorphic coefficients have spectral asymptotics; ES Type I/II correlate divisor-class counts at N and N + (shift) across slices.

title: Holowinsky–Soundararajan: sieve + subconvexity combo for 'large on average, so not zero' at one form
connection: Holowinsky–Soundararajan proved mass equidistribution for holomorphic Hecke forms by combining two weak methods (sieve bounds for shifted sums, Soundararajan's weak subconvexity) that each fail alone; ES's pointwise lower tail resists every single method.
why: Template for 'two complementary partial methods cover all cases' — e.g. one method for p with many small factors in 4Cp+1, another for the rest.

title: Nelson / Michel–Venkatesh subconvexity for Type I class-group twisted sums
connection: Subconvexity for GL₂ twists by class-group characters (Michel–Venkatesh) gives equidistribution of Heegner/CM objects; Type I class-group sums at discriminant −16d are such twisted sums.
why: Michel–Venkatesh-type bounds are what Duke-type equidistribution at a single discriminant needs.

title: Waldspurger / Gross–Zagier toric periods for Type I class-group sums
connection: Waldspurger's formula expresses squares of toric periods as central L-values; Type I counts involve sums over ideal classes of a quadratic order tied to p.
why: A toric-period interpretation would make ES Type I counts nonnegative combinations of L-values (positivity built in).

title: Hecke-like transport between f(n) and f(ℓn)
connection: Solutions for n lift to ℓn (multiplicativity); a Hecke operator T_ℓ on solution sets would also need an adjoint pulling solutions from ℓn back to n, which is exactly the missing direction for primes.
why: If solution counts satisfied Hecke-type relations (f(ℓ²n) related to f(n), f(ℓn)), one could deduce f(p) > 0 from composite data.

connection: MSS proved bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist by showing the expected characteristic polynomial's root bounds the root of some member (interlacing families); ES needs one good member (certificate) among a family.

connection: Strömbergsson–Venkatesh study the distribution of the smallest solution of linear congruences via equidistribution of lattices; ES certificates are small solutions of congruences with modulus tied to p.

connection: Browning–Vinogradov make Ratner equidistribution effective on ASL(2) to count affine-lattice events; ES Type I/II with a fixed shift (p) are affine-lattice problems (L + p·v).

connection: Katz: Kloosterman angles at a fixed prime modulus equidistribute w.r.t. Sato–Tate as the argument varies; ES fixed-modulus counts (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS) reduce to Kloosterman-type sums.

connection: Rudnick–Soundararajan prove lower bounds for moments of L-function families by a simple Hölder trick; ES needs lower bounds for a count of certificates.

connection: HRS give sharp upper bounds for fractional moments of ζ; small-moment control is equivalent to lower-tail information for log-normal-like quantities.

connection: Nicolas–Serre describe coefficients of modular forms mod 2 via a nilpotent Hecke algebra; the repo PROVED complement pairing makes level counts even and R(p)/2 mod 2 looks like a fair coin.

connection: Fourier interpolation reconstructs f from values at √n and f̂ at √n; ES lattice reformulations have theta series whose coefficients count certificates.

connection: PST proved André–Oort via canonical height bounds; the Cayley cubic/Markoff CM dictionary in the repo (cayley_markoff_cm) relates special points to CM data.

connection: Theta lifts produce modular generating functions of traces/cycle counts; Borcherds products give automorphic forms with prescribed divisors. ES counts across p could be coefficients of such a lift if they are traces over class groups.

connection: Dedekind-sum reciprocity s(a,c)+s(c,a) = (a/c + c/a + 1/(ac))/12 − 1/4 relates HJ continued fractions of a/c and c/a; ES certificates have HJ/CF data (DEDEKIND_ES).

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord (Tao–Vu, Nguyen–Vu) for signed subset products hitting −1
connection: For squarefree N = ∏ℓ_i, the e-slice quotient ab⁻¹ (ab | N) is ∏ ℓ_i^{ε_i} with ε_i ∈ {−1,0,1} — a signed 'Littlewood–Offord walk' in (ℤ/e)^×. Inverse LO theorems say a walk concentrates on one value only if the steps are structured (lie in a small GAP/subgroup).

title: Target-Davenport constants for I3 at small t: forcing −1 from enough prime factors
connection: In (ℤ/t)^× with t ≤ 20, a sequence of prime factors of tn+1 of length ≥ D(G) has a nonempty subproduct ≡ 1; the I3 event needs a divisor ≡ −1, so a 'target' Davenport constant is the forcing threshold.
why: Combined with 'tn+1 has many prime factors for some t ≤ T' (provable for most n?), could give I3 for many n deterministically.
first_step: Compute target constants for G = (ℤ/t)^×, t ≤ 30, and the fraction of n where some t ≤ 30 has ω(tn+1) above the threshold.
refs: Geroldinger–Halter-Koch, Non-Unique Factorizations (2006)

title: U(n) sporadic set {105, 2961, …} vs Rickards–Stange 'squares + finitely many sporadic' templates
connection: Rickards–Stange proved a 'squares + 15 sporadic' theorem for a fat orbit Ψ via long character sums; U(n) fails at odd squares + 6 sporadic ≤ 10⁹.
why: Comparing exact mechanisms tells whether U(n) is a thin-fibre or fat-fibre problem — calibration for which tools could prove U(n)'s sporadic list complete.
first_step: Factor the sporadic n (105 = 3·5·7, 2961 = 3²·7·47, …) and look for a common local feature (all divisible by 3? all ≡ 1 mod 8?).
refs: Rickards–Stange (as cited in ES_APPROACH_GENERATORS.md §1)

title: Brauer–Manin for the pencil S_{n,k} at k = −4 (sibling failures {2,9,21,165,945,1197})
connection: The repo proved a BM obstruction on S_{n,k} for positive squares k; at k = −4 failures exist but no invariant is known; Colliot-Thélène–Xu style integral BM with negative k is untried.
why: Explaining sibling failures by a BM class would refine the zero-law calibration and test whether ES-type failures are always 'lottery'.
first_step: Compute Br S_{n,−4} and evaluate the candidate quaternion classes at the failing n.
refs: Z52_BANKED.md §1
Colliot-Thélène–Xu, Brauer–Manin obstruction for integral points of homogeneous spaces and representation by integral quadratic forms, Compositio 145 (2009)

title: Function-field transfer of T1: odd squares in 𝔽_q[T] and the reciprocity obstruction
connection: T1 (no Type I/II at odd squares) should have a function-field analogue with polynomial reciprocity; FF_ODD_ABSENCE/FF_STERILE memos study function-field sterility.
why: In function fields the obstruction might be explained by monodromy, giving a conceptual T1 proof that could suggest a 'prime T1' test.
first_step: Verify T1 for squares of irreducible polynomials over 𝔽_3, 𝔽_5 numerically and compute the monodromy of the certificate cover at a square.
refs: FF_ODD_ABSENCE.md

title: 8/n and k/n siblings: Kahn–Kalai threshold across the numerator k
connection: Varying the numerator k (k/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z) changes the expected solution count; Schinzel–Sierpiński-type problems are open for each k ≥ 4.
why: A threshold picture across k (where 'almost all' becomes 'all') calibrates ES's position.
first_step: Compute failure counts of k/n for k = 4..12, n ≤ 10^6 (excluding trivial obstructions) and fit expected-count vs failure-rate curves.
refs: Elsholtz, Sums of k unit fractions, Trans. AMS 353 (2001)

title: Kloosterman/KMS bounds applied to the I3 count averaged over t
connection: I3's divisor event involves tn+1 with class −1 mod t; averaging over t ≤ T at fixed n gives Kloosterman-type sums with modulus t (small).
why: Fixed-n averages over t is the I3 analogue of fixed-p averages over C — test bed for bilinear Kloosterman input.
first_step: Write Σ_t Σ_{d | tn+1} 1_{d ≡ −1 (t)} via Fourier in d mod t and identify the Kloosterman sums.
refs: Kowalski–Michel–Sawin, arXiv:1511.01636

title: Gaussian ES_Q1 count growth log³N vs log²N: Lang–Weil / local densities explanation
connection: z52 found ES_Q1 counts grow like log³N (EVIDENCE) against the board's log²N; integral-Manin-type predictions depend on the rank of the relevant Picard/boundary data over ℚ(i).
why: A geometric explanation (extra boundary component splitting over ℚ(i)) would validate the log-power heuristics used for ES itself.
first_step: Compute the Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel exponent for U_n over ℚ(i) vs ℚ (Galois action on boundary/nodes) and compare with 3 vs 2.
refs: Z52_BANKED.md
Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel, Igusa integrals and volume asymptotics in analytic and adelic geometry, Confluentes Math. 2 (2010)

title: Maynard–Tao weights over the slice index e at fixed p
connection: At fixed p the slices N_e = (p+e)/4 are consecutive integers; MT weights over admissible tuples of slices could force several slices to be 'structured' (e.g. have a small prime factor in a chosen class) simultaneously.
why: Fixed-p, average over e: legitimate without averaging over p — and MT weights are designed for consecutive-integer tuples.
first_step: Choose an admissible k-tuple of slice offsets and compute (numerically) the MT weighted proportion of windows where ≥ 2 slices succeed.
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł for divisor-class functions on the slice window (N, N+H) at fixed p
connection: The Type II slices are the short interval [p/4, p/4 + H]; MR-type theorems give almost-all-short-interval behaviour, but here the interval is one specific interval (fixed by p).
why: Precisely localises the B2-type gap as 'one specific short interval near p/4' — any 'all short intervals' theorem for the divisor-class function would prove ES.
first_step: Check the strongest known 'all intervals of length H' result for multiplicative functions (e.g. Teräväinen/MR 'every interval' results for smooth numbers) and compare H with ES's polylog window.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Ann. Math. 183 (2016)

title: Smooth numbers in all short intervals (Matomäki–Radziwiłł; Teräväinen) → smooth slice existence
connection: MR prove every interval [x, x + C√x] contains x^ε-smooth numbers? (check exact statement); a smooth slice N_e has many small prime factors and likely succeeds.
why: An 'every interval' smooth-number theorem is a pointwise tool; the slice window near p/4 is short (polylog?) so the needed length must be compared.
first_step: Check the exact current record for smooth numbers in every short interval and compare with the number of slices available at p (e < some bound).
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), §1 (smooth numbers in short intervals)

title: Green–Sawhney-type Type II information for p² + 4c²d with d prime
connection: Restricting to prime d makes p² + 4c²d a sparse polynomial family close to Green–Sawhney's p² + nq² setting.
why: Sub-family selection to reach a known bilinear estimate; the count loses only a log factor.
first_step: Measure how often Type I certificates with d prime exist at p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Green–Sawhney, arXiv:2410.04189

title: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth-style traces for I3's t-family (closed geodesics of discriminant t²n²+…)
connection: (tu−1)(tv−1) = tn+1 relates to binary forms of discriminant depending on (t,n); traces over these classes could be mock-modular generating functions.
why: Same speculative mechanism as for ES₅, but I3's single free parameter t makes the family cleaner.
first_step: Identify the binary quadratic form whose representation gives I3 at (t,n) and compute its discriminant.
refs: Duke–Imamoḡlu–Tóth, Ann. Math. 173 (2011)

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD graphs for I3 overlaps across t
connection: I3 events for different t at fixed n share prime factors through gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) | (t−t′)… structure; GCD graphs quantify such overlaps.
why: Second-moment control at fixed n over t is the key missing step; GCD-graph compression is designed for that.
first_step: Compute gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) statistics for t,t′ ≤ 100 at the hardest I3 n values.
refs: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard, arXiv:1907.04593

title: Rosser–Iwaniec semi-linear sieve for I3 at t = 4: 'tn+1 has a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4)'
connection: At t = 4, the I3 event needs a divisor of 4n+1 that is ≡ −1 (mod 4) (plus size constraints): it fails iff all prime factors of 4n+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) — a semi-linear sifted set of density ≍ (log n)^{−1/2}.
why: Exact density of the t = 4 failure set; combining t = 4, 8, 12 … failures gives a sieve-dimension computation for I3's exceptional set.
first_step: Compute the joint failure probability for t ∈ {4, 8, 12, 16} under independence and compare with data.
refs: Iwaniec, Rosser's sieve, Acta Arith. 36 (1980)

title: Chen–Stein Poisson approximation for I3 counts at fixed n
connection: I3 counts at fixed n over t, u, v are sums of weakly dependent divisor events; Poisson approximation predicts P(count = 0).
why: I3 is verified to 10^9 with a known largest exception 2 433 600 — calibrates Poisson-model predictions of the largest exception.
first_step: Fit the Poisson model on n ≤ 10^8 and predict the largest exception; compare with 2 433 600.
refs: Arratia–Goldstein–Gordon (1989)

title: Extreme-value prediction of ES's 'last hard prime' scale from sibling data
connection: Siblings with known last exceptions (I3: 2 433 600; U(n): 978145?) calibrate extreme-value models mapping expected count μ(n) to the largest failing n.
why: If the same model predicts ES's last failure below 2 (i.e. none), it quantifies P(ES false) consistently across siblings.
first_step: Fit log P(fail at n) ≈ −μ(n)·κ on siblings, then evaluate Σ_{p > 10^18} exp(−κ μ(p)).
refs: Z52_BANKED.md T2–T4

title: Bhargava-style 'average over a family then sieve to the subfamily' for ES over n in APs
connection: Bhargava's method: count over a big family with geometry of numbers, then sieve to squarefree/maximal subfamilies via uniformity estimates; ES averaged over n in APs mod M is a sieve to sub-families.
why: Uniformity estimates ('tail' bounds) are exactly what pass from averages to subfamilies like Mordell-hard classes.
first_step: Compute averaged ES counts over n ≡ r (mod 840) for each Mordell-hard r and check uniformity in r of the main-term constant.
refs: Bhargava–Shankar, Binary quartic forms having bounded invariants, and the boundedness of the average rank of elliptic curves, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Lean formalisation of T1 (odd squares have no Type I/II solutions)
connection: T1 is a short reciprocity argument (ET Prop 1.6; Yamamoto); formalising it in Lean is a contained project.
why: T1 is the single most-used test in the campaign; a machine-checked version prevents subtle scope errors (cf. the R290 coprimality repair).
first_step: Write T1 in Lean 4 with Mathlib's Jacobi symbol API and formalise the coprime Type I/II definitions.
refs: Elsholtz–Tao, Counting the number of solutions to the Erdős–Straus equation on unit fractions, J. Aust. Math. Soc. 94 (2013)

title: SAT/ILP search for a 'prime T1': a non-square class where all certificates of bounded shape fail
connection: A 'prime T1' (structured family of primes with no Type I/II certificates of a bounded shape) is the campaign's sought disproof-shape; SAT/ILP can search residue systems where all bounded-shape certificates fail.
why: Either finds sterile families to a given depth or certifies none exist below a modulus — sharp data for the sterility question.
first_step: Encode depth-K sterility for certificate shapes with C ≤ K as a CRT-consistency SAT instance and search moduli up to 10^6.
refs: STERILE_LOWER.md

title: Davies-style ML on sibling failures: which local features predict S_{n,−4} and ES_Q1 failures?
connection: Sibling failures (S_{n,−4}: n ≡ 0 mod 3 odd failures; ES_Q1: Im n ≡ 1 mod 4 cell) were partly explained by low-count cells; attribution on a classifier could find further features.
why: If failures are fully explained by local count-lowering features, the lottery reading is strengthened.
first_step: Train a classifier on n ≤ 10^5 with local features (n mod q, Legendre symbols) to predict S_{n,−4} counts; inspect feature importance.
refs: Z52_BANKED.md

title: Murmuration-type averages of I3 counts against n mod t
connection: Average I3 counts as a function of n's residue pattern across t could show oscillations analogous to murmurations.
why: Exposes hidden structure that residue-class fits might miss.
first_step: Plot normalised I3 counts averaged in windows vs n/X and residues mod 840.
refs: Zubrilina, arXiv:2310.07681

title: Hypergraph-container count of 'ES-closed failure sets' compatible with all identities up to modulus M
connection: The set of possible failure sets (divisor-closed, avoiding identity-covered classes) can be enumerated/counted via containers; its entropy measures how constrained a counterexample must be.
why: Disproof-shape calibration: if very few configurations survive, a counterexample is highly structured.
first_step: Count, for n ≤ 10^4 restricted to Mordell-hard residues, the number of divisor-closed sets avoiding identity coverage up to modulus M.
refs: Balogh–Morris–Samotij, JAMS 28 (2015)

title: Kahn–Kalai / Park–Pham on the I3 random model (small groups, many events)
connection: I3's events per n are many (t ranges) with small moduli; threshold theory could predict exactly when 'expected ≥ 1' implies 'present w.h.p.'.
why: I3 is proved-false-free beyond 2 433 600 in data; matching threshold predictions is a sanity test of the method before ES.
first_step: Compute expectation thresholds for I3 events at n ~ 10^6–10^9 in the random model.
refs: Park–Pham, arXiv:2203.17207

title: Effective Chebotarev in the ES Type I ray class fields (explicit success density per (c,d))
connection: For fixed (c,d), the density of primes p having a Type I certificate with that (c,d) and a prime f is a Chebotarev density in a field tied to (c,d); summing gives M_BM's constant.
why: Explicit densities let one compute the exact main term and the variance contributed by each (c,d).
first_step: Compute the Chebotarev density for (c,d) ∈ {(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)} via PARI and compare with empirical frequencies.
refs: Lagarias–Odlyzko, Effective versions of the Chebotarev density theorem (1977)

title: Quantitative Hilbert irreducibility (Cohen; Castillo–Dietmann) for ES certificate covers
connection: Quantitative HIT bounds the number of specialisations where a Galois group drops; ES certificate covers over the p-line have Galois groups whose specialisations at p determine certificate existence.
why: If the cover's Galois group stays large at all but few p, Chebotarev-type positivity follows for most p — and exceptional p are 'thin sets'.
first_step: Compute the Galois group of a single Type I certificate cover (fixed c,d) over ℚ(p) and its thin-set exceptions.
refs: Castillo–Dietmann, On Hilbert's irreducibility theorem, Acta Arith. 180 (2017)

title: Thin-set (Serre) structure of ES-hard primes
connection: Serre's thin sets (images of rational points under covers of degree ≥ 2) have density zero with explicit counts; if 'p fails all certificates of shape ≤ K' were a thin set, its count would be ≪ X^{1/2}.
why: A thin-set description of depth-K hard primes would give power-saving depth-K exceptional bounds.
first_step: Test whether depth-K hard primes cluster on values of polynomials (e.g. squares, quadratic polynomials) by fitting.
refs: Serre, Topics in Galois Theory (1992), ch. 3

title: Expander walk sampling + Ramanujan graphs for Monte Carlo estimates of M_BM constants
connection: Expander-walk Chernoff bounds give sharp concentration for Monte Carlo with few random bits; estimating Euler-product-type constants and certificate densities by sampling primes benefits.
why: Minor computational gain; listed as a concrete use of Ramanujan-graph technology.
first_step: Implement expander-walk sampling of primes in [X, 2X] and compare variance of estimates of mean f(p) with i.i.d. sampling.
refs: Gillman, A Chernoff bound for random walks on expander graphs, SIAM J. Comput. 27 (1998)

title: Spectral sparsification / effective resistance on certificate dependency graphs
connection: Spielman–Srivastava sparsification approximates graphs by sparse ones preserving quadratic forms; the Janson Δ is a quadratic form on the certificate dependency graph.
why: Allows computing/approximating Δ for huge certificate families at large p.
first_step: Compute Δ exactly for p ~ 10^7 and approximately via sparsification at p ~ 10^12.
refs: Spielman–Srivastava, Graph sparsification by effective resistances, SIAM J. Comput. 40 (2011)

title: Kelley–Meka sifting for pooled multi-slice certificates
connection: Pooling several slices with a common modulus e (e.g. N_e and N_{e′} with e | stuff) creates larger generating sets; KM-type density increments find large structured pieces in the pooled divisor sets.
why: Pooling is the natural escape from B2's 'one integer' constraint; additive-combinatorial structure theorems are the tool to exploit pooled sets.
first_step: Identify ES certificate shapes that legitimately combine prime factors of two different p-tied integers in one group, if any (check SIGNED_REFACTOR.md / COMPOSITION_ES.md).
refs: Kelley–Meka, arXiv:2302.05537
COMPOSITION_ES.md

title: Bloom unit-fraction method for 'k/n with prescribed smooth denominators' — 3-term specialisation test
connection: Bloom's method finds subsets of a dense set with reciprocal sum exactly 1 by Fourier analysis over many terms; the 3-term case loses all averaging.
why: Testing where the method breaks as the number of terms drops to 3 is a clean B3-type calibration.
first_step: Track, in Bloom's argument, the minimal number of terms needed for the Fourier step and how it scales.
refs: Bloom, arXiv:2112.03726

title: Mixing of the greedy/odd-greedy Egyptian map as a Markov chain on residues
connection: The map n ↦ remainder after subtracting the greedy unit fraction acts on residues; as a Markov chain its mixing describes the distribution of remainders (cf. Tao's Syracuse analysis).
why: Mixing estimates give 'almost all' success of fixed-depth greedy-with-choice algorithms and pinpoint residue traps.
first_step: Compute the transition matrix of the remainder residue mod M for the 2-step greedy-with-choice ES search and its spectral gap.
refs: Tao, arXiv:1909.03562
